summary:
Botswana decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct through its own courts. The High Court struck down the colonial-era provisions of Penal Code Section 164(a) and (c) on 11 June 2019 in Letsweletse Motshidiemang v Attorney General, and the Court of Appeal upheld that judgment on 29 November 2021, writing that such laws "incentivise law enforcement agents to become key-hole peepers and intruders into the private space of citizens." The repealed paragraphs were formally struck from the statute book in March 2026 by the Rectification of the Laws (Penal Code) Order, 2026.

Before repeal the offence covered both heterosexual and homosexual sodomy and carried up to seven years' imprisonment. Prosecution was rare: the U.S. State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report recorded that police "did not target same-sex activity" that year and reported no violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2011.

Penal Code Section 167, which addresses same-sex conduct between women, remains in force. In the Universal Periodic Review of May 2023 (43rd session), Botswana declined Canada's recommendation to repeal Section 167 and also declined a recommendation to introduce an administrative process for legal gender recognition; the outcome records that "a clear administrative process... was yet to be introduced" (para 570).

Legal gender recognition has been won case by case rather than granted by statute. In September 2017 the High Court held that the Registrar of National Registration's refusal to change a transgender man's gender marker violated his constitutional rights to dignity, privacy, freedom of expression, equal protection, freedom from discrimination and freedom from inhumane and degrading treatment, and ordered the state to change his identity documents from female to male (ND v Attorney General).

In December 2017 the High Court ordered the government to recognise the gender identity of transgender woman and activist Tshepo Ricki Kgositau, who obtained a female identity card after a four-year legal battle and gender confirmation surgery in December 2016. She dedicated the victory to "every single trans diverse person in Botswana."

In June 2019 the High Court ruled that "sex" in Section 3 of the Constitution must be "generously and purposively interpreted" to include sexual orientation. Legal commentator Carmel Rickard wrote that this gives LGBTQ Batswana "an even stronger, constitutionally-based argument" against discrimination.

A Southern Africa Litigation Centre analysis of 20 May 2024 assessing Botswana's precedent wins (the 2016 Court of Appeal order registering LEGABIBO, the 2017 identity-document ruling and the 2021 decriminalisation) concludes that implementation across Botswana and Namibia "has not been satisfactory so far."

A draft constitutional amendment under consideration in June 2024 would add discrimination protection for intersex persons and people with disabilities. In deliberations that month the Minister of Labour and Home Affairs told legislators to keep "intersex" and "same-sex" distinct, and civic groups criticise the wider review process.

Statements by senior officials have run in sharply different directions. In February 2011 the Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly said he would have those who practise homosexuality killed if he had the power. In September 2016 President Ian Khama deported the American anti-gay pastor Steven Anderson, stating "we don't want hate speech in this country." In November 2018 President Mokgweetsi Masisi acknowledged that people in same-sex relationships "have been violated and have also suffered in silence for fear of being discriminated" and deserved protection. Former President Festus Mogae told the BBC that he had instructed police not to arrest or harass gay people during his ten years in office, while declining to change a law he said would lose him an election. LEGABIBO and activists called the government's 2019 appeal an "affirmation of persistent homophobia and transphobia."
tangentialFactors:
Social tolerance, as measured by Afrobarometer, rose from 43% in 2016 to 50% in 2021 welcoming or not being bothered by a homosexual neighbour. That figure describes the country as a whole rather than attitudes toward trans visitors specifically, and it leaves a substantial minority outside the tolerant group.

Botswana's record is cited together with Namibia's by regional litigators, who found implementation of comparable precedent judgments unsatisfactory in both countries; a visitor crossing the border should expect the two jurisdictions to be assessed side by side rather than assumed equivalent.

The 2011 U.S. State Department Human Rights Report documents same-sex conduct as criminalised at that time and records societal discrimination against LGBT people. The same report's wider assessment covers violence against women, prison conditions and discrimination against the San, which frames the general human-rights environment rather than trans-specific risk.

The decriminalisation judgment came only after a government appeal, which LGBT organisations characterised as an affirmation of persistent homophobia and transphobia. Court victories in this jurisdiction have therefore been contested by the state rather than conceded.
localsOnly:
LEGABIBO is the country's principal LGBTIQ+ organisation, running advocacy, awareness campaigns and sexual-health and HIV work including a World AIDS Day 2017 commemoration in Bobonong. Its site carries Coming Out, Law & Constitution and Help & Support resources, and it operates as legally registered community infrastructure, registration having been won in the 2016 Court of Appeal order.

The draft constitutional amendment adding intersex and disability discrimination protection is being processed through a wider constitutional review whose conduct civic groups criticise. The Minister of Labour and Home Affairs instructed legislators in June 2024 deliberations to keep "intersex" and "same-sex" as separate categories, which shapes how protection language is drafted for residents.

Because no administrative gender-recognition procedure exists, residents must litigate each marker change individually. The 2017 rulings are therefore precedents available to citizens, not an entitlement that can be exercised at a registry counter.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Botswana has since introduced the administrative gender-recognition process it declined at the May 2023 Universal Periodic Review is unresolved in this inventory; no source after that session addresses it.

The current status of the draft constitutional amendment first reported in June 2024, including whether the intersex discrimination provision was adopted, is unresolved and not sourced here.

Whether the March 2026 Rectification of the Laws (Penal Code) Order has been verified against a primary gazette is not sourced; the claim rests on a secondary account of the deletion of paragraphs (a) and (c) of Section 164.

No source in this inventory records a prosecution under Section 167, so its enforcement risk for visitors is not sourced. Equally, no source reports violence against a trans visitor specifically; the 2011 finding of no reported violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity relates to that year only.
